summary:
What if the first step toward establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon or Mars was not to leave Earth, but to understand it better?

GeoAnalog is an interactive geospatial research platform developed by Maxwellianos to identify potential terrestrial analogs for future lunar and Martian exploration.

Using open data from NASA and partner institutions, we developed quantitative methods to compare planetary environments through topography, temperature, albedo, vegetation, precipitation, and spectral characteristics.

Our expanded global dataset contains 691,035 geographical cells across 727 regions, producing a ranking of 200 potential analog sites. Additionally, our detailed Colombian case study evaluated 18 terrestrial, lunar, and Martian regions through 72 pairwise comparisons. The Tatacoa Desert achieved a topographical Planetary Analog Index (PAI) of 92.02/100 against the Mars Pathfinder landing site.

Through interactive planetary globes, explainable similarity metrics, and scientific visualizations, GeoAnalog aims to identify promising natural laboratories for testing exploration technologies while recognizing the physical limitations of terrestrial analogs.

Before exploring other worlds, we must rediscover our own.

GEOANALOG

Exploring Other Worlds Through Our Own

THE BEGINNING OF OUR RESEARCH

Throughout human history, curiosity has driven us to cross the boundaries of the unknown. We have explored the depths of our oceans, reached the highest mountains, sent robotic explorers to distant planets, and left our first footprints on the Moon.

Today, humanity faces an even greater challenge: establishing a sustainable presence beyond Earth.

However, reaching another world is only the beginning. Where should we land? What geological conditions will we encounter? How can we prepare our instruments, robotic systems, and exploration strategies for environments that are fundamentally different from our own?

Perhaps part of the answer lies beneath our feet.

Our planet contains an extraordinary diversity of environments. From the frozen landscapes of Antarctica and Greenland to the immense deserts of Africa and Asia, and the volcanic formations of the Andes, Earth offers natural laboratories that share certain characteristics with extraterrestrial environments.

But what if we could identify these similarities beyond their visual appearance? What if we could quantify them through mathematics, satellite observations, and planetary science?

This is where our research begins.

DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPOSAL

GeoAnalog is a scientific and computational project developed by Maxwellianos to identify, characterize, and visualize potential terrestrial analogs for future lunar and Martian exploration.

Our proposal integrates open scientific data, remote sensing, planetary geology, statistical analysis, and interactive geospatial visualization.

Rather than assuming that environments are analogous simply because they look alike, we investigate measurable physical characteristics that allow us to establish quantitative relationships between different planetary surfaces.

Our research combines three complementary components:

  • A global search for potential terrestrial analogs.
  • A detailed scientific characterization of selected Colombian environments.
  • An interactive planetary visualization platform.

Together, these components establish a framework for exploring similarities and differences between Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

EARTH AS A NATURAL LABORATORY

Testing space exploration technologies directly on extraterrestrial surfaces presents enormous technical, economic, and logistical challenges.

Terrestrial analog environments provide opportunities to investigate specific planetary conditions before deploying scientific instruments and technologies beyond Earth.

Deserts can contribute to the study of exposed soils, aridity, and terrain mobility. Volcanic landscapes can provide opportunities for geological investigations. Polar regions and high-altitude environments can support research into cold conditions and operational challenges.

However, no terrestrial environment can reproduce every physical characteristic of another celestial body.

For this reason, GeoAnalog approaches planetary analogs as environments that share specific measurable characteristics rather than as identical replicas of extraterrestrial worlds.

GLOBAL SEARCH FOR PLANETARY ANALOGS

One of the main objectives of our research is to expand the identification of terrestrial analog candidates beyond traditionally recognized locations.

Our expanded global database contains 691,035 geographical cells distributed across 727 regions.

These regions encompass different geographical and environmental conditions, including:

  • Antarctica, Greenland, and the Canadian Arctic.
  • The Andes, Atacama Desert, and South American highlands.
  • The Sahara and other African deserts.
  • The Arabian Peninsula and Middle Eastern arid regions.
  • The Tibetan Plateau and Central Asian deserts.
  • North American deserts and volcanic environments.
  • Iceland, Australia, and other geologically diverse territories.

Our global methodology evaluates physical and environmental descriptors, including elevation, slope, terrain roughness, surface temperature, thermal variability indicators, albedo, precipitation, vegetation, and an estimated emissivity contrast.

By processing these variables, we generated a geographically diversified ranking of 200 potential terrestrial analog sites: 100 candidates for lunar exploration and 100 candidates for Martian exploration.

Known analog environments were also considered as references within our broader research.

HOW DOES GEOANALOG WORK?

1. Scientific data acquisition

GeoAnalog incorporates open scientific resources from NASA, ESA, USGS, Copernicus, and other scientific institutions.

Our research combines digital elevation models, orbital observations, spectral measurements, geological maps, meteorological information, and planetary climate models.

The diversity of these datasets allows us to investigate different physical dimensions of terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.

2. Topographical characterization

Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) provide numerical representations of planetary surfaces.

For our detailed regional analysis, we used NASADEM for Earth, Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) observations for the Moon, and the combined HRSC–MOLA elevation model for Mars.

Eighteen nominal study windows of 10 × 10 km were processed at a common spatial resolution of 200 meters per pixel.

From these models, we extracted topographical descriptors such as:

  • Elevation and relative elevation.
  • Terrain slope.
  • Local and robust relief.
  • Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI).
  • Topographic Position Index (TPI).
  • Terrain aspect.

These variables provide a quantitative representation of terrain morphology, allowing us to investigate similarities between environments with different geological histories.

3. Environmental characterization

Our terrestrial research incorporates satellite observations and meteorological datasets to characterize surface temperature, precipitation, vegetation, land cover, solar energy, atmospheric pressure, humidity, and wind conditions.

NASA POWER, MODIS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, CHIRPS, and ESA WorldCover provide complementary environmental information.

These variables contribute to understanding the extent to which terrestrial environments reproduce specific conditions relevant to planetary exploration.

4. Geological and mineralogical characterization

The composition of planetary surfaces represents another important dimension of analog research.

For Earth, our detailed Colombian analysis incorporates geological information from the Colombian Geological Survey and spectral observations from Sentinel-2 and NASA's Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT).

EMIT observations allow us to investigate spectral signatures associated with surface materials and evaluate their corresponding uncertainty and quality indicators.

For Mars, we processed spectral parameters from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM), aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Our global analysis also explores emissivity contrast derived from ASTER observations and a literature-based approximation of equivalent spectral composition for lunar and Martian targets.

These approaches provide complementary information about surface materials. However, spectral indicators and library matches are not equivalent to confirmed chemical concentrations or laboratory mineral identification.

5. Planetary thermal characterization

Thermal properties play an important role in understanding planetary environments.

For Mars, we investigated thermal inertia products from the Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES) and brightness temperature observations from the Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS).

For the Moon, we processed data from the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment aboard NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

These data allow us to investigate annual subsurface temperatures, maximum surface temperatures, and modeled conditions of water ice stability.

The global comparison also incorporates modeled Martian surface temperatures from the Mars Climate Database.

Differences between observed, modeled, and derived thermal quantities are explicitly considered when interpreting the results.

QUANTIFYING THE SIMILARITIES BETWEEN WORLDS

GeoAnalog implements two complementary scientific approaches for calculating planetary similarities.

Planetary Analog Index (PAI)

For our detailed Colombian case study, we developed the Planetary Analog Index, a dimensionless numerical indicator based on topographical characteristics.

The methodology uses Z-score standardization and weighted Euclidean distance across six terrain descriptors.

The resulting distance is transformed through the following expression:

PAI = 100 / (1 + D)

Where D represents the weighted Euclidean distance between two environmental feature vectors.

The index approaches zero as the distance increases and reaches 100 for identical feature vectors.

A higher PAI indicates greater similarity within the evaluated topographical parameters.

This index does not represent a percentage of physical equivalence between planets.

Global similarity model

For the international search, we implemented a separate similarity model based on physically motivated tolerances and weighted numerical distances.

Differences between environmental variables are normalized according to their respective tolerances, allowing quantities with different physical units to contribute to a common comparison framework.

The resulting distance is transformed into a similarity score:

S = exp(−D)

This model also incorporates data coverage requirements, geographical separation between selected candidates, and sensitivity analysis to investigate how changes in variable weights influence the rankings.

By maintaining different analytical approaches, GeoAnalog can investigate detailed terrain similarities while also considering broader environmental constraints.

COLOMBIA: REDISCOVERING OUR OWN PLANET

Colombia is internationally recognized for its biodiversity. However, its geological, geographical, and climatic diversity also represents an opportunity for planetary science.

As part of our detailed regional investigation, we selected six Colombian environments:

Tatacoa Desert: Exposed sedimentary formations and erosion-driven terrain.

La Guajira: Arid coastal environments, exposed soils, and aeolian formations.

La Candelaria Desert: Sedimentary formations and distinctive erosional landscapes.

Nevado del Ruiz: High-altitude volcanic terrain and glacial features.

Nevado Santa Isabel: High-altitude volcanic and glacial environments.

Puracé Volcano: Volcanic materials and complex mountainous terrain.

These environments were compared against six Martian regions and six lunar regions associated with potential exploration objectives.

Our analysis generated a total of 45,000 elevation cells and 72 Earth-to-Moon and Earth-to-Mars comparisons.

One of our most promising topographical results was obtained between the Tatacoa Desert and the Mars Pathfinder landing site, with a PAI of 92.02 out of 100.

Tatacoa also obtained scores of 84.16 against Gale Crater and 83.88 against Jezero Crater.

For the lunar component, La Candelaria achieved a PAI of 55.96 against Connecting Ridge, while Puracé achieved 53.55 against Leibnitz Beta Plateau.

These results suggest opportunities for further scientific investigations into Colombian planetary analog candidates.

GLOBAL RESEARCH RESULTS

Our expanded global research identified 200 geographically diversified potential terrestrial analog locations.

Among the highest-ranked candidates for lunar exploration were regions in northern Greenland, northern Ellesmere Island, and the Changtang Plateau in Tibet.

For Martian exploration, some of the highest-ranked candidates were located in the Egyptian Western Desert, Libya, and Sudan.

The lower scores obtained when incorporating environmental constraints reveal an important scientific result: a terrestrial environment can exhibit meaningful topographical similarities while still presenting considerable differences in its broader physical conditions.

Rather than interpreting these differences as failures, GeoAnalog uses them to identify the specific dimensions in which terrestrial analogs may be scientifically useful.

ADDITIONAL SCIENTIFIC RESULTS

Our complementary regional analyses include:

  • 18 selected EMIT acquisitions, corresponding to 36 mineral identification and uncertainty files.
  • 222 regional aggregates of provisional spectral library matches.
  • Qualified CRISM spectral observations across five Martian regions.
  • 36 THEMIS scenes, of which 31 passed preliminary quality checks.
  • 5,079 Diviner facets intersecting six lunar study windows.
  • Thermal inertia characterization using TES observations.
  • Geological characterization of six Colombian environments.

These products represent complementary scientific investigations. Their incorporation into a unified planetary similarity model remains an opportunity for future development and validation.

AN INTERACTIVE WAY TO EXPLORE OTHER WORLDS

Science becomes more powerful when its findings can be explored and understood.

To make our research accessible, we developed an interactive web platform that allows users to explore Earth, the Moon, and Mars through three-dimensional planetary globes, satellite imagery, geographical information, and comparative visualizations.

The integrated web prototype was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, and CesiumJS.

The application includes an interactive comparison system, scientific information about selected environments, configurable similarity weights, rankings, multilingual support, and guided exploration.

The integrated web version uses an initial global database of 163,998 geographical cells across 43 regions, with 71 exported sites. An expanded research dataset extends this analysis to 727 regions, with full integration of the latest scientific products representing the next stage of development.

Through this approach, GeoAnalog seeks to transform complex scientific data into an intuitive and educational experience.

TECHNOLOGIES AND DEVELOPMENT

GeoAnalog was developed through the integration of scientific computing, geospatial analysis, web development, and cloud infrastructure.

Our technological resources include:

  • Python, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and scikit-learn.
  • Rasterio, GDAL, PyProj, and Shapely.
  • Matplotlib and Google Earth Engine.
  • React, TypeScript, Vite, and CesiumJS.
  • Git and GitHub.
  • Microsoft Azure Static Web Apps, Terraform, and GitHub Actions.

The project processes scientific formats including GeoTIFF, NetCDF, HDF, PDS, CSV, GeoJSON, and JSON.

Our source code, processing methodologies, and scientific products are documented in our project repository:

https://github.com/Mabeltranpe1/NASA_SPACE_APPS_2026

SCIENTIFIC LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DEVELOPMENT

Earth cannot completely reproduce lunar or Martian gravity, atmospheric conditions, radiation exposure, geological evolution, or thermal cycles.

Our methodology also recognizes differences in spatial resolution, instrumental capabilities, temporal coverage, measurement uncertainty, and data compatibility.

The calculated similarity scores are exploratory indicators rather than definitive certifications of planetary analog suitability.

Future development will focus on improving scientific validation, propagating measurement uncertainty, harmonizing environmental variables, expanding geographical coverage, and integrating complementary geological, mineralogical, and thermal products into the platform.

INNOVATION AND EXPECTED IMPACT

GeoAnalog brings together planetary science, remote sensing, mathematical modeling, geospatial analysis, and interactive technology to explore the scientific relationship between Earth and other worlds.

Our purpose is to support the identification of promising natural laboratories, contribute to the preparation of future exploration missions, encourage the use of open scientific data, and promote interest in planetary science.

We believe that planetary exploration should not begin exclusively on distant worlds, but also in the extraordinary diversity of our own planet.

Space exploration is not only about discovering what lies beyond Earth. It is also about rediscovering our own world through a different scientific perspective.

Before building a future on another planet, we must learn to recognize its possibilities within our own.

Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure

The Maxwellianos team used Super Intelligence tools, including OpenAI ChatGPT, Claude and Codex, to support ideation, scientific research, data analysis and interpretation, code development, debugging, repository auditing, and technical documentation.

These tools assisted the development process. The scientific datasets originate from NASA and other scientific institutions, while the implemented similarity metrics are based on mathematical and statistical methods. GeoAnalog does not currently incorporate a trained artificial intelligence or machine learning model as a core functionality.

GeoAnalog — Exploring Other Worlds Through Our Own.
